<ExternalIntegrationHeader slug="dlna" />

:::info

La documentación de esta integración la escribe su autor y, por ahora, solo está disponible en inglés.

:::

Control the DLNA / UPnP renderers of your home (TV, amplifier, speaker, streamer) and play the
content of your media servers (Plex, Jellyfin, Emby, MiniDLNA, a NAS…) from Gladys. Everything stays
on your local network: no account, no cloud.

## Requirements

- Gladys 5.1.0 or later.
- The renderers and servers on the same network as Gladys. A device on another network (VLAN, other
  subnet) can be added by hand, see below.
- On a renderer, DLNA must be enabled: it is sometimes called "DLNA", "UPnP", "Media renderer",
  "Play to" or "AllShare" in its settings, and some TVs only answer when they are on (not in
  standby).

## Adding your devices

1. Install the integration, then open its **Discovery** tab: Gladys searches the network and lists
   the renderers and the media servers it found. Run the search again with the button if a device is
   missing (a TV must be on).
2. Add the devices you want. A **renderer** gets the playback commands; a **media server** gets no
   feature, but it then appears in the scene actions.
3. Some devices are both: a Denon amplifier, for instance, is a renderer and a small media server.
   The server is then listed with "(media server)" after its name.

**Language of names and messages** (English, French, German or Spanish): Gladys keeps the names
of a device once it is added, so pick the language in **Configuration** before adding the devices.
It is also the language of the error messages of device commands and scene actions (Gladys does not
tell an integration the language of its user).

**A device that is not found**: SSDP discovery only works on the network of Gladys. Find the URL
of the UPnP description of the device (in the documentation of the device or the server: MiniDLNA serves
`http://<address>:8200/rootDesc.xml`, a Denon/HEOS amplifier
`http://<address>:60006/upnp/desc/aios_device/aios_device.xml`). Check it with the **Test a
description URL** action, then add it to **Description URLs** in the configuration and run the
search again.

## The renderer device

| Feature        | What it does                                                     |
| -------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Play, Pause    | Starts or resumes, pauses (stops when the renderer cannot pause) |
| Stop           | Stops the playback                                               |
| Previous, Next | Previous or next track (of the queue, see below)                 |
| Volume         | 0 to 100 %, mapped to the range the renderer declares            |
| Mute           | Toggles mute                                                     |
| Playback state | 1 while playing, 0 otherwise (paused, stopped, off)              |
| Now playing    | "Artist — Title" as the renderer describes it, "—" when nothing  |
| Notification   | Used by the core "Play a notification" scene action              |

Volume and Mute only appear when the renderer has them. The device works with the core **Music**
widget of the dashboard (previous, play/pause, next, volume).

**What the device plays some other way** (Spotify Connect, AirPlay, Chromecast, an HDMI input…):
**volume** and **mute** are the device's own, so Gladys sets them whatever the source. For example,
a soundbar playing Spotify, even on a free account, has its volume controlled from Gladys (seen on
a Sennheiser AMBEO Soundbar). The playback state, the now-playing title and the transport commands,
on the other hand, only follow what is played **over DLNA**: during a Spotify session, the device
shows "stopped".

The state is refreshed every few seconds while playing, every 15 seconds otherwise. A renderer
that is off shows the **unreachable** badge and is checked once a minute; when it comes back on
another address, the integration finds it again by itself (a network search, at most every 5
minutes).

## Scenes

**Triggers**

- **DLNA playback started**, **DLNA playback paused**, **DLNA playback stopped**: pick a renderer,
  or leave it empty for any. The following actions can use `{{triggerEvent.data.renderer}}`,
  `{{triggerEvent.data.title}}`, `{{triggerEvent.data.artist}}` and `{{triggerEvent.data.album}}`.
  Typical use: dim the lights when the TV starts playing a film, turn them back on when it stops.
  A renderer that is switched off fires nothing (it is not a "stop"), and neither does the short
  gap between two tracks of a queue.

**Actions**

- **Play a media server on a DLNA renderer**: pick the renderer and the server, then what to
  search:
  - _Anything_: titles, artists and albums containing the text, then a folder of that name;
  - _Title_, _Artist_, _Album_ (an album plays in track order);
  - _Folder_: a folder name (`Jazz`), or a path from the root of the server (`Music/Jazz`). The
    tracks of its sub-folders are included. Use the **Browse a media server** action of the
    configuration to find the paths.

  Then choose to play everything in order, everything shuffled, or the first result only, and
  optionally a volume. A search that takes more than 75 seconds (a huge library on a server that cannot search) stops with an error: give a narrower one, such as a folder path. The action returns whether something was found, the number of tracks queued
  and the first title, for the following actions.

- **Play a URL on a DLNA renderer**: a web radio, a sound or an announcement file, by its http(s)
  URL, with an optional title and volume. The URL must be reachable by the renderer itself. Left
  empty, the title is the name the web radio gives itself (its `icy-name` header, or else the title
  on air when the stream starts), and the URL as a last resort: the integration asks the stream
  once, for at most 2.5 seconds, without downloading it.

- **Play a DLNA favorite**: plays one of the favorites of the configuration (see below) on a
  renderer, with an optional volume. It returns whether it started and the name of the favorite.

**Queue**: a DLNA renderer plays one media at a time. For an album or a folder, the integration
keeps the list and hands the tracks over one after the other (without a gap when the renderer
supports it). Next and Previous walk the list. The queue stops when something else is played on
the renderer, and it only advances while Gladys and the integration run.

**Announcements**: the core **Play a notification** action works on the renderers (it needs Gladys
Plus for the text-to-speech). It plays at the current volume (the core does not pass its volume to
the integrations), and the previous media is not resumed afterwards. To set the volume of an
announcement, place a device control action on its Volume feature before it.

## Favorites

In **Configuration**, the **Favorites** part holds up to 8 favorites, each one a numbered group of
fields:

- **Name**: shown on the button (24 characters fit). Left empty, the favorite is named after the
  host of its URL or after its search.
- **URL**: a web radio or a file, by its http(s) URL; **or** a search on a **media server**: the
  name of the server as it appears in Gladys (part of it is enough; empty when only one server is
  added), what to search by (anything, title, artist, album, folder or playlist), the search
  (`Abbey Road`, `Music/Jazz`), and how to play what is found (in order, shuffled, the first
  result). When both are filled, the URL wins. A favorite with neither is ignored.

The server is named rather than picked in a list on purpose: Gladys refuses to save a configuration
whose list holds a device that no longer exists, and a deleted server would block every later
change of the configuration.

## Dashboard

Add the **DLNA player** widget and pick a renderer in its settings: it shows the title, the album,
the state, the queue position, mute, a live volume gauge, and four buttons (play/pause, stop,
volume − and +, by steps of 5 %).

Add the **DLNA favorites** widget, pick a renderer and the favorites to show: one button per
favorite, four at most per widget (Gladys allows four buttons in a widget). Add several widgets to
reach more favorites. Left empty, the widget shows the first four favorites of the configuration.
It also shows the favorite the renderer holds now, with its state, and marks its button with a
check: it stays until something else is played on the renderer.

## Configuration actions

- **Test a description URL**: reads a description URL and tells what it holds.
- **Browse a media server**: lists the folders and tracks of a server, from the root or from a
  path (`Music/Albums`).

## Sonos, Samsung, LG

Sonos speakers, Samsung TVs and LG webOS TVs have their own Gladys integrations, which do more than
DLNA (groups, sources, applications). This integration still sees them when they offer DLNA: it is
useful to play media from a server or announcements, next to their own integration.

## What has been checked on real hardware

- **Checked for real on a Denon AVR-S650H** (playback, pause, volume, mute, stop, browsing of the
  built-in server): an http stream plays, the position advances, pause and resume work, the volume
  set in Gladys is the volume of the amplifier (15 in Gladys is MV15), mute is set and read back,
  stop stops, and the built-in media server is browsed. The amplifier wakes from standby by itself
  on a command. Its description, service descriptions and state answers are replayed by the tests.
- **A renderer in standby can take up to a minute to start**: measured on the Denon, it accepts
  the media and the Play command, gives no usable answer for about 12 seconds while it wakes up,
  then stays stopped and ignores Play for about 40 more seconds before it starts. The integration
  therefore follows every start for up to 75 seconds, in the background: it waits while the
  renderer does not answer, presses Play again every 5 seconds while it is stopped (and loads the
  media again if needed), restarts once a playback cut right after it started, and stops following
  as soon as another command or media comes in. Scene actions answer as soon as the renderer
  accepted the command; a start that never comes is written in the logs of the integration. https
  streams play like http ones.
- **Checked by a user on a Sennheiser AMBEO Soundbar**: found by itself at install time, volume set
  from the widget, including during a Spotify Connect session.
- **Not checked on real hardware yet**: the play queue and its gapless transitions, the network
  search run by Gladys, searching a real media server (MiniDLNA, Plex, Jellyfin), the favorites and
  their widget, and the station name read from a real web radio. They are
  covered by tests on simulated devices built from public formats. Please report any device that
  misbehaves, with the logs of the integration.

## Troubleshooting

- **Nothing in the Discovery tab**: check that the devices are on and on the same network as
  Gladys; read the logs of the integration (`Discovery: N SSDP answer(s)…`). Add a description URL
  by hand otherwise.
- **"Nothing to play over DLNA"** (or nothing to pause, stop, no next track): the renderer has no
  DLNA media loaded, and may be playing another source (Spotify, AirPlay, an HDMI input…). Start a
  media from Gladys, or use the app of that source. Stop is still sent, since some devices stop the
  other source too. The logs of the integration keep the UPnP code the renderer answered (for
  instance `Play failed: 701 Transition not available`).
- **Another refusal** reads as its meaning (format not accepted, media not reachable, renderer in
  standby or busy…); its UPnP code is in the logs of the integration. The message follows the
  language of the configuration, except on the widget buttons for "nothing over DLNA", shown in
  the language of the user.
- **A web radio shows its URL instead of its name**: the stream does not give a name (no `icy-name`
  header), or did not answer within 2.5 seconds. Fill the title of the scene action, or make it a
  favorite with a name.
- **A file or a radio does not play**: the renderer must support its format, and reach its URL
  itself. A renderer in standby may take about ten seconds to start: the integration waits for it.

## Cómo instalar DLNA en Gladys

1. En Gladys, abre **Integraciones**: DLNA aparece en el catálogo junto a las integraciones nativas, con una insignia de comunidad.
2. Haz clic en **Instalar**. Gladys descarga la imagen Docker (`ghcr.io/guim31/gladys-dlna:1.1.0`), la ejecuta en un entorno aislado del núcleo y genera la interfaz de la integración (dispositivos, descubrimiento y configuración).
3. Abre la pantalla de **Configuración** de la integración, rellena los parámetros y guarda.
4. También puedes instalarla directamente desde la URL de su repositorio: [https://github.com/guim31/gladys-dlna](https://github.com/guim31/gladys-dlna).

DLNA requiere Gladys `>=5.1.0`. El catálogo de Gladys se actualiza cada hora, así que una nueva versión está disponible como máximo una hora después de publicarse.

¿Todavía no usas Gladys? Es gratuito y de código abierto: [sigue la guía de instalación](/es/docs/) para empezar.

## Sobre las integraciones externas

DLNA es una **integración externa**: una integración comunitaria empaquetada como contenedor Docker y publicada en GitHub. Gladys la instala con un clic y la ejecuta en un entorno aislado del núcleo. La publica y mantiene [guim31](https://github.com/guim31), no el equipo principal de Gladys.
